young.html: Alfred North Whitehead was a mathematician who became a philosopher. He asked: why did modern science start when and where it did? And does science tell us everything about the world?

Think of a sunset at the beach. A scientist can describe it with numbers: the angle of the sun, the length of the light waves, the temperature of the air. All true! But the warm colors, the sound of the waves and the feeling of the evening are left out of the numbers. Whitehead said we should not forget that the numbers come from the real evening, not the other way round.

young.name: gb-whitehead-abstraction
young.cap: Climb the ladder of abstraction: each step up keeps less of the real evening, and becomes more useful for calculating.

young.html: What the numbers leave out. Choose something you love: a dog, a pie, a song. Write three facts about it a scientist could measure. Then write three things about it that no measurement catches. Are both lists true?

full.html: Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) taught mathematics in Cambridge and London for decades and wrote Principia Mathematica with his former student Bertrand Russell. In 1924, aged 63, he moved to Harvard to teach philosophy. Science and the Modern World grew from his Lowell Lectures in Boston in 1925. It is a history of how science shaped modern thought, and a philosopher's criticism of the picture of nature that science seemed to leave behind.

full.text: Where the faith in science came from

full.html: Why did modern science arise in Europe in the 1500s and 1600s? Whitehead points to an attitude older than any theory: the confident belief that nature is orderly and can be understood.

full.text: I mean the inexpugnable belief that every detailed occurrence can be correlated with its antecedents in a perfectly definite manner, exemplifying general principles. Without this belief the incredible labours of scientists would be without hope.
full.author: Alfred North Whitehead
full.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter I

full.html: Where did that belief come from? His answer, which historians still discuss:

full.text: My explanation is that the faith in the possibility of science, generated antecedently to the development of modern scientific theory, is an unconscious derivative from medieval theology.
full.author: Alfred North Whitehead
full.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter I

full.html: He means the medieval teaching that the world was made by a rational God, so its order could be trusted and searched out. Whitehead adds that Greek thought and the new habit of careful observation were needed too.

The scientists of the 1600s pictured nature as bits of matter moving in space and time. Colors, sounds and smells were put "in the mind" rather than in nature. Whitehead sums up, with irony, what that picture implies:

full.text: Nature is a dull affair, soundless, scentless, colourless; merely the hurrying of material, endlessly, meaninglessly.
full.author: Alfred North Whitehead
full.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter III

full.html: That picture, he argues, mistakes a useful abstraction for the full concrete reality, an error he names the fallacy of misplaced concreteness. Bits of matter at points are what we get when we leave most of experience out; they are not more real than the experience they came from.

full.name: gb-whitehead-abstraction
full.cap: What each level of description keeps and leaves out.

full.html: Whitehead looks to the Romantic poets, Wordsworth and Shelley, as witnesses that nature as we meet it is full of value and life. His own alternative, the "philosophy of organism," treats the world as made of interconnected events and processes rather than lumps of stuff, a view he worked out fully in Process and Reality (1929).

full.text: The greatest invention of the nineteenth century was the invention of the method of invention.
full.author: Alfred North Whitehead
full.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter VI

full.html: He means the research laboratory and the habit of turning science into technology on purpose. The last chapters ask how religion and science can each learn from the other, and what a society needs to make progress without losing its balance.

The book was widely read and helped make the history of science a serious subject. Historians still debate Whitehead's claim about medieval theology: some have built on it, while others stress the role of Greek and Islamic science, the rise of crafts and trade, or argue that science and religious authority were sometimes in conflict. His "process" philosophy remains influential among some philosophers and theologians, though less so in mainstream academic philosophy, which followed Russell and Wittgenstein.
Thinking Whitehead was against science. He was a mathematician who loved it; he objected to a particular philosophy that treated science's abstractions as the whole of reality.

items: Galileo and Descartes sorted qualities into those "in" things (shape, motion) and those in the mind (color, taste); Whitehead's Chapter III examines the result.
Plato's Timaeus pictures a world ordered by a divine craftsman; Whitehead admired it.
Aquinas and the medieval thinkers held that faith and reason do not conflict; Whitehead traces the scientific attitude back to that confidence.
Bergson, the earlier rung, also attacked the habit of mistaking our cuts in reality for reality itself.

questions: Describe your kitchen as a scientist would, then as a poet would. Which is truer?
Why might believing that the world is orderly help someone become a scientist?
What is something important that cannot be measured?
Whitehead said the 19th century invented the "method of invention." What inventions came from laboratories?
Is a map of a place more real than the place? What is the map good for?
